notes: Check batch 2026-10-23-check-2: four skill runs (haiku-1, haiku-2, sonnet-1, sonnet-2), no opus, all rc 0, each model_id matching its tier (each transcript's assistant messages name only that model), head 4215aa3 with uncommitted true and one skill_hash. git diff d04061d HEAD -- idiomatic-elixir/ is empty, so the only change since the sixth sweep is the uncommitted new rule that git diff HEAD -- idiomatic-elixir/SKILL.md shows; every transcript contains its heading text ("only when its pattern and body are each one plain term"), so the runs read it. Each run made one Read, of SKILL.md, and no reference file; expected reads is none beyond SKILL.md, so all four meet it. In the scratch folder all four files pass mix format --check-formatted and compile with elixirc --warnings-as-errors (Elixir 1.20.3). Doctests: haiku-1 1 of 1, haiku-2 1 of 1, sonnet-1 3 of 3, sonnet-2 2 of 2.

New rule "Keep a `->` clause on one line only when its pattern and body are each one plain term", graded against its text and the case's new bullet. Deciding sentence: "A pattern that holds a binary, a guard or nesting, or a body that holds a nested call or a string built with `#{}`, goes on the line after the `->`." Runs violating: 1 of 4 (sonnet-1). Runs exercising it (any case, cond, with ... else, fn or receive clause): 4 of 4; every clause in the batch is a case clause (no cond, fn, receive or with ... else). Clauses that decide the verdicts, verbatim: sonnet-1 line 158: {:ok, value} when is_binary(value) and value != "" -> {:ok, value}; line 166: {:ok, value} when is_binary(value) or is_nil(value) -> {:ok, value}; line 174: {:ok, value} when is_integer(value) and value >= 0 -> {:ok, value} (guarded patterns kept on one line, in string_field/2, optional_string_field/2 and amount_field/2). The same three helpers in sonnet-2 put the body on the next line with blank lines between clauses: line 143: {:ok, value} when is_binary(value) ->, line 156: {:ok, value} when is_binary(value) or is_nil(value) ->, line 169: {:ok, amount} when is_integer(amount) and amount >= 0 ->. haiku-2 does the same in string_field/2, amount_field/2 and failure_reason/1: line 106: %{^key => value} when is_binary(value) ->, line 119: %{^key => value} when is_integer(value) and value >= 0 ->, line 132: %{"failure_reason" => reason} when is_binary(reason) or is_nil(reason) ->. haiku-1's typed_field/3 breaks both clauses: line 132: {:ok, value} ->, line 133: if predicate.(value), do: {:ok, value}, else: {:error, {:invalid_field, key}} (a body with nested calls, on the next line) and line 135: :error ->. The one-line clauses left in the batch are the DateTime.from_unix/1 case in haiku-1 (lines 121-122), haiku-2 (lines 94-95) and sonnet-1 (lines 121-122): {:ok, created_at} -> {:ok, created_at} and {:error, _reason} -> {:error, {:invalid_field, "created"}}; the patterns are one-level tuples and the second body is a nested tuple of literals, not a nested call, so they are clean. Under a reading that counts a nested tuple body as not plain, haiku-1, haiku-2 and sonnet-1 would each be violated on that line; the rule's text lists only nested calls and #{} strings for bodies, and SKILL.md's own examples keep {:error, reason} -> {:error, {:unreadable, reason}} on one line, so I did not count it.

Head-rule bullets, violating runs out of 4. (1) The parsing head matches the keys it requires with a clause below: 0 of 4 violated, 4 of 4 exercised; every run has def parse(%{"id" => ..., "type" => ..., "created" => ..., "data" => ...}) with def parse(_payload), do: {:error, :invalid_payload} below it. haiku-1 and sonnet-1 bind type (and haiku-1 created) that the guard does not read, clean by presence; haiku-2 binds each key as _ beside = payload. (2) No selecting pattern moved into a body: 0 of 4 violated, 4 of 4 exercised. (3) Clutter: 0 of 4 violated. haiku-1's four-clause parse_event/4 (lines 73-85) takes id, created and data as positional arguments, not fields destructured from a matched value, and the fourth clause underscores them, so they are not bound in every clause; the type mappers (event_kind/1, parse_type/1) and data dispatchers (event_fields/2, parse_data/2) match literals and take data whole; wrapped heads (haiku-1 lines 63-64, sonnet-1 lines 103-104, sonnet-2 lines 98-99) move only the guard.

Read required keys: haiku-2 is the only break. Its parse/1 head matches "type", "created" and "data" as _ (line 35) and the body then reads them with bracket access (lines 37-39), the map[:key] form for keys the head itself makes required. haiku-1's data["failure_reason"] (line 105) reads a key Payment leaves out of @enforce_keys, an optional key, as the previous sweep allowed. The other paragraphs (body pattern on one key, dot chains, get_in/1, Map.fetch/2) are not exercised beyond Map.fetch-based readers.

Closest calls, graded to the previous standard. Match every expected shape: sonnet-1 line 129 and sonnet-2 line 115, defp parse_data(_payment_type, data), do: parse_payment(data), parse every atom other than :refund_created as a payment, the shape 2026-10-22-d graded violated in skill-sonnet-2 and 2026-10-21 before it, so both are violated; the type mappers' catch-alls in haiku-1 (line 85), haiku-2 (line 51) and sonnet-1 (line 117) also receive a non-string type ("type" => 123 gives {:unsupported_event, 123}, verified), checks only as before; sonnet-2 guards is_binary(type) in the head. Comments: haiku-1's lines 70-72 describe the split between parse_event/4 and the field parsers and then give its reason (a known type with a bad field reports the field); 2026-10-22-d graded the same comment shape in skill-haiku-1 and skill-haiku-2 as explaining why, so clean; line 99 says why failure_reason is read optionally (absent or nil means no failure reason), also clean. The with rule: sonnet-2 line 101, {:ok, created_at} <- DateTime.from_unix(created), lets {:error, :invalid_unix_time} pass through without a private normalizing function; earlier sweeps counted only else blocks and one-step withs under this rule, so it is clean (counted, Sonnet would be violated on the with rule); it goes into checks as an error that names no field. haiku-1's event/4 (lines 87-91) takes the already-computed parse result as its first with step; it has two steps and no else, so clean. Naming: haiku-1's parsed_data and predicate, haiku-2's kind, attrs and data_map/1 are not counted, as before. Outside the list: haiku-1's if inside a case (lines 131-133) goes under Keep functions short, as before; sonnet-2's struct literal inside {:ok, ...} (lines 123-130) is not a call argument and is not counted.

Probe of 20 payloads, run in the scratch folder against each file. In all four: an unknown type gives {:unsupported_event, type}; a known type without amount gives {:missing_field, "amount"}; a string or nil amount gives {:invalid_field, "amount"}; refunds without refund_id or payment_id name that field; a payload missing id or data, or a non-map payload, gives :invalid_payload. Differences: a negative amount is accepted by haiku-1 only; an integer failure_reason is accepted by haiku-1 and rejected by sonnet-1 and sonnet-2 (haiku-2 ignores it on payment.succeeded); a string created gives :invalid_payload in haiku-1 and sonnet-2 (guards) and {:invalid_field, "created"} in the others; an out-of-range created gives {:invalid_field, "created"} in three runs and {:error, :invalid_unix_time} in sonnet-2; a non-string id gives {:invalid_field, "id"} and list data {:invalid_field, "data"} in haiku-2 and :invalid_payload in the others; a non-string type gives :invalid_payload in sonnet-2 and {:unsupported_event, 123} in the others.

Compared with the sixth sweep's skill runs (2026-10-23 at d04061d; that sweep had Opus, this batch has none): Read required keys moves from Haiku clean to violated (haiku-2's bracket reads after a head match); Match every expected shape moves from Sonnet clean to violated (the parse_data/2 payment catch-all, in both Sonnet runs); Comments moves from Sonnet violated to clean (doctests pass in both Sonnet runs). The multi-clause rule, atoms, the with rule, the return-tuple rule, the struct rule and Naming stay clean in Haiku and Sonnet.
